title: Lumepay Raises $6M Pre-Seed to Scale African Cross-Border Payments
snippet: Lumepay has disclosed a $6 million pre-seed round to expand its cross-border payments and digital asset infrastructure across Africa, following regulatory clearance to enter Kenya. The post Lumepay Raises $6M Pre-Seed to Scale African Cross-Border Payments appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
South African cross-border payments provider Lumepay has disclosed a $6 million pre-seed funding round backed by founder-led angels and domestic fintech investors. Closed at the start of 2026 alongside approximately $10 million in capital float secured to anchor client liquidity, the capital supports the company’s rail-agnostic B2B payments and digital asset infrastructure for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), corporates, and financial institutions.

The disclosure comes amid rapid structural shifts across global money movement, with worldwide cross-border payment volumes projected to reach $320 trillion by 2032. Across Africa, businesses are increasingly moving away from fragmented correspondent banking chains toward faster settlement networks—a trend underscored by transaction values on the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) more than doubling in 2026 compared to the prior year.

Multi-Rail Infrastructure and East African Expansion

Led by CEO Harry Huang, chief operating officer Luc Varejes, and chief legal and compliance officer Tatenda Nhemachena—who bring more than 20 years of combined industry experience alongside a broader executive team—Lumepay operates at the intersection of conventional banking rails, foreign exchange depth, and stablecoin liquidity.

Lumepay co-founders from left to right, COO, Luc Varejes, CEO Harry Huang, chief legal and compliance officer, Tatenda Nhemachena

Following the pre-seed close, the company executed several commercial rollouts across the continent:

Digital Asset Trading: Launched Lumetrade, its institutional digital asset and stablecoin trading venue, in April 2026.

Cross-Border Payments Platform: Rolled out its broader B2B cross-border payments platform across Africa in June 2026.

Kenyan Market Entry: Secured regulatory clearance from the Central Bank of Kenya in October 2026 to launch local operations, enabling Kenyan enterprises to settle international supplier invoices in currencies including Chinese yuan (CNY), US dollars (USD), and Indian rupees (INR) while executing intra-African transfers.

Lumepay and Lumetrade are currently live across the West African CFA franc zone (XOF), Central African CFA franc zone (XAF), Nigeria (NGN), Ghana (GHS), Tanzania (TZS), Malawi (MWK), Mozambique (MZN), and Kenya (KES), with additional regulatory approvals pending to expand local payment capabilities. Looking ahead, the firm is prioritizing expansion across Southern, West, and Central Africa, specifically targeting Malawi, Mozambique, and the XOF and XAF regions.

“The future of cross-border payments isn’t traditional finance or stablecoins; it’s a combination of both, backed by the FX depth to make them work for real businesses,” stated Harry Huang. “That’s how we’ve built Lumepay: a rail-agnostic platform that works at the intersection between the two… Our integrated approach addresses the real drivers of friction: fragmentation, liquidity inefficiency and execution risk.”

“In the months since the raise, we’ve turned plans into working products: diversified and reliable liquidity; a platform that handles cross-border payments end to end; a growing network of partners and payment rails; and regulatory clearance in South Africa and Kenya, together with licensed partners across Francophone West and Central Africa,” added Luc Varejes.

Tier-One Banking Partnerships and Regulatory Architecture

To support institutional transaction volumes, Lumepay has established direct banking and regulatory infrastructure across key jurisdictions:

South African Payment Rails: Lumepay (Pty) Ltd operates as a registered Third-Party Payment Provider (TPPP) in South Africa, partnering with Nedbank as its sponsoring bank for domestic rand (ZAR) merchant collections and disbursements.

Regulated Digital Asset Dealing: Lume Trade (Pty) Ltd holds a Category I Financial Services Provider (FSP No. 54670) license covering intermediary services in crypto assets, derivatives, and deposits, utilizing a banking relationship with Standard Bank to facilitate ZAR deposits and withdrawals for institutional clients.

North American Registrations: Lumepay Limited is registered with Canada’s FINTRAC as a Money Services Business (MSB) and with the Bank of Canada as a payment service provider under the Retail Payment Activities Act.

“Banks are rigorous about who they work with, and they should be,” noted Tatenda Nhemachena. “Working with Nedbank and Standard Bank across our two businesses reflects the compliance standards we have built from day one.”

Having deployed its pre-seed capital to establish enterprise-grade security, wallet infrastructure, banking relationships, and licensed regional partnerships, Lumepay is now entering its growth phase and laying the groundwork for a Series A round.

title: Global Payments faces industry pricing pressure
snippet: While analysts point to an increasingly competitive environment for the processor, the company is still trying to raise prices.
fullText:
Global Payments and other processors face an increasingly competitive market, with rising pricing pressures forcing some businesses in the ecosystem to consider consolidation.

Global Payments has touted increased merchant acceptance of its Genius point-of-sale services brand, but now it may be trying to force through price hikes in an increasingly competitive market.

The payments processing company is seeking to implement a new $699 annual fee for its merchant clients next month, according to a merchant consultant who posted a portion of a Global Payments letter on LinkedIn. 

“Worldpay, now part of Global Payments, is introducing a $699 annual fee, with the first charge hitting merchant statements this December. Yes, another one,” Merchant Cost Consulting Partner Matt Rej said in the LinkedIn post last week. “And this is on top of the other increases we've already seen from Worldpay this year.”

Rej questioned, and poked fun at, the reasoning Global Payments provided for the increase, pointing to the company’s letter saying: “Government and industry regulations have had a significant impact on system requirements in the payment processing industry.”

The Atlanta-based company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Nonetheless, in its third-quarter earnings press release last week, the company acknowledged “increased competition in the markets in which we operate.”

Global Payments pricing moves come less than a year after it completed its $24.25 billion purchase of the merchant services company Worldpay, which could give the company stronger pricing power in the industry. In the third-quarter report, Global Payments reported that the Genius brand, which was launched last year, was placed at 65% more merchant locations, compared to the year-earlier period, and bookings more than doubled.   

As the Genius brand gains traction, the company is reportedly considering selling itself off to one of its largest shareholders, private equity firm GTCR, and the investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. GTCR is acquainted with Global Payments partly because it was one of the companies that sold it the Worldpay assets.

Any fee increases by POS service providers are increasingly met with pressure from younger financial technology companies building a presence in the market with newer technologies. As a result, some legacy companies that provide payments services to merchants, including behemoth Fiserv, the new entrant Shift4 and the Dutch company Adyen, are feeling a competitive crunch.

Point-of-sale services firm PayCompass said in September that it had merged with two other firms and the CEO at the merchant services provider Butter Payments said last month that the company had sold its assets to an unnamed buyer.

While analysts who follow Global Payments praised the company’s progress in integrating Worldpay into its operations and luring merchants to the Genius brand, they noted the increasingly competitive market. As such, price increases may be a tough sell, particularly as merchants face consumers stretched by inflationary pressures. 

Analysts at the investment firm William Blair raised concerns about Global Payments technology being capable of competing with new fintechs.

“While sales metrics appear strong, we argue Genius is simply not a competitive offering from a technology standpoint and will not become material enough to durably accelerate consolidated organic growth,” the analysts said in a Thursday note to their clients, acknowledging the brand’s third-quarter growth.

Other analysts who follow the company also pointed out the competitive intensity in the market in commenting on Global Payments results.

“The Payments industry is very competitive with both existing and emerging competition,” analysts for TD Cowen told clients in a note Thursday. “All of our companies face the risk of being unable to capture market share or having their business models become commoditized by newer entrants in the market. Additionally, our companies are levered to consumer spending and therefore are exposed to general economic conditions.”

Analysts who follow the company for the investment firm R.W. Baird called out the difficulties for raising prices at this time across the industry. “Pricing pressure is a constant threat, and new fintechs have become competitive threats as well,” analysts at the Baird Equity Research arm said in a Thursday note. 

A sale to private owners might relieve some of the pressure of operating in the publicly traded market, with its focus on quarterly reports. Still, the analysts at William Blair last week gave the deal less than a 50-50 chance of being completed, partly because of the debt that Global Payments has in the wake of its Worldpay deal.

In a prior Oct. 30 note focused exclusively on the reports of a potential Global Payments sale, the William Blair analysts said that some $22 billion of debt at the company “could be an impediment, especially in a rising rate environment.”

The William Blair analysts posited that they could be wrong about the chances of the sale. If they are, they forecast that other “debt-laden” publicly traded companies in the industry, including Shift4 Payments and Fiserv, will see “pressure to sell will ratchet up dramatically, setting up what could be the final wave of industry consolidation.”

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: Mercuryo Launches Swaps with 1,400 Routes Across 24 Digital Tokens
snippet: Mercuryo's new Swaps product offers fixed-quote token conversion across 24 assets and 21 blockchain networks, though it is unavailable in the US, UK The post Mercuryo Launches Swaps with 1,400 Routes Across 24 Digital Tokens appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Mercuryo, the London-headquartered payments infrastructure platform, has launched Swaps, a token conversion product that lets users move holdings between 24 digital assets across 21 blockchain networks. The company says the product covers 1,400 distinct swap routes, offers fixed quotes and zero slippage, and is executable in a single click.

The asset list runs from the major tokens by market capitalisation, including bitcoin (BTC), ether (ETH) and the two dominant stablecoins, Tether’s USDt and USDC, through to more speculative names including Dogecoin, Pepe, Shiba Inu and Kaspa. Supported networks include Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, Solana, BNB Smart Chain, TON and the XRP Ledger, among others. Liquidity is sourced through an unnamed cryptocurrency exchange that Mercuryo says applies anti-money-laundering controls, though the company has not disclosed the counterparty.

The geographic restriction

The most commercially significant detail in the announcement is a geographic carve-out: Swaps is not available to users in the United States, the United Kingdom or the European Economic Area. That restriction covers the three largest regulated digital-asset markets by institutional participation and removes a substantial proportion of global retail trading volume from Mercuryo’s addressable user base for this product.

The exclusion is likely a regulatory precaution rather than a commercial choice. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority requires cryptoasset businesses to register and applies financial promotions rules that constrain how token conversion services can be marketed. Across the EEA, the Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation (MiCA), which came fully into force in late 2024, creates a harmonised but demanding licensing and disclosure framework for crypto-asset service providers. The US remains fragmented across Securities and Exchange Commission, Commodity Futures Trading Commission and state-level money-transmission regimes, and enforcement actions against token swap venues have put overseas providers on notice. Rather than clear those hurdles immediately, Mercuryo appears to be launching in markets where the compliance overhead is lower, keeping its options open for regulated-market entry at a later stage.

Market context

Arthur Firstov, chief business officer at Mercuryo

Arthur Firstov, Mercuryo’s chief business officer, pointed to the company’s own on-ramp transaction data as the commercial rationale for the product. Mercuryo’s figures for the first half of 2026 show stablecoin transactions rising from 43 per cent to 60 per cent of total on-ramp volume during a period when bitcoin fell 33.2 per cent and ether dropped 47.3 per cent. The company interprets this as evidence that retail users are actively managing portfolio exposure rather than passively holding, creating demand for a low-friction conversion tool.

The token swap segment is well-established. Decentralised exchanges such as Uniswap and centralised platforms including Binance Convert and Coinbase‘s Simple Trade all offer similar functionality, often with broader asset coverage and deeper liquidity. Mercuryo’s proposition is the fixed-quote model, which removes slippage uncertainty at the cost of locking in a spread, and integration with its existing on-ramp and payment infrastructure for users already on the platform. Whether that bundled positioning is sufficient to attract meaningful volume outside the UK, US and EEA remains to be tested.

The company counts Trust Wallet, MetaMask, Revolut, Mastercard and Visa among its partners, which gives it distribution into existing user bases that could provide an early adoption channel for Swaps. The unnamed liquidity provider and the lack of any disclosed fee or spread structure are gaps that institutional observers will note before assessing the product’s competitiveness.

title: Glovo and PragmaGO Bring Embedded Lending to Polish Merchants
snippet: PragmaCash is now available to Glovo's restaurant and retail partners in Poland, offering financing of up to PLN 100,000 within one business day. The post Glovo and PragmaGO Bring Embedded Lending to Polish Merchants appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Glovo and PragmaGO have extended their embedded lending partnership to Poland, making PragmaCash financing available to the delivery platform’s network of local merchants from October 2026. Poland is the third market for the tie-up, following rollouts in Spain and Romania.

The product targets the small and independent businesses that make up a significant share of Glovo’s merchant base: restaurants, cafés, grocery stores, florists and pharmacies. Merchants can apply entirely online, receive a credit decision within minutes, and access financing of up to PLN 100,000 (approximately EUR 23,000), with funds transferred to their account within one business day. The financing carries no stated restriction on use, meaning it can cover stock purchases, seasonal staffing or any other operational need.

The commercial case

Joanna Budzik-Lister, VP strategic partnerships at PragmaGO

Joanna Budzik-Lister, VP strategic partnerships at PragmaGO, pointed to internal data as the backbone of the commercial argument. “Our data show that companies using this type of financing achieve year-on-year turnover that is 28% higher than companies that do not use it,” she said. The comparison is drawn from PragmaGO’s Merchant Cash Advance cohort, tracking the twelve months before and after a financing application.

Diana Hangartner, commercial director at Glovo Poland

Diana Hangartner, commercial director at Glovo Poland, framed the partnership as extending the platform’s existing value proposition beyond logistics. Running a local business now requires the capacity to act quickly on market opportunities, she said, and access to capital through the platform itself reduces friction for merchants already operating inside the Glovo ecosystem.

PragmaGO reported that nearly 24,000 entrepreneurs used its embedded lending product in 2025, drawing a combined PLN 872 million (approximately EUR 200 million) in financing across its markets. That figure represents a 66% year-on-year increase, though the release did not break down volume by country.

Market context

Embedded lending for gig-economy and delivery platform merchants has become a competitive category across Europe. The model is structurally attractive: a platform that processes a merchant’s transaction data already holds the most reliable proxy for repayment capacity, making underwriting faster and cheaper than a traditional bank loan application. Several other platform lenders and banking-as-a-service providers are pursuing the same merchant segments, including through partnerships with food-delivery and e-commerce marketplaces.

PragmaGO’s positioning is notable in that it is not a pure-play technology intermediary but a regulated financial institution with three decades of SME lending experience in Poland, operating since 1996. The group’s structure, which includes a Romanian digital factoring subsidiary, a Spanish embedded-finance unit and a Croatian operation, suggests a deliberate multi-market expansion model rather than an opportunistic single-deal play. That breadth of regulated experience may give it a compliance advantage as EU supervisors pay closer attention to the non-bank lending layer sitting inside consumer-facing platforms.

Poland’s SME financing market is large and historically underserved by retail banks for short-term working capital, which creates structural demand for faster, data-driven alternatives. The Glovo distribution channel gives PragmaGO a captive merchant population with verifiable revenue data, while Glovo gains a value-added service that deepens merchant retention without requiring it to hold a lending licence itself. The next test is whether transaction volumes in Poland match the trajectory seen in Spain and Romania, and whether the product can be scaled without a material rise in default rates as the borrower pool widens.

title: Behind the Idea: Redvest
snippet: Redvest founder Anya Ozmen on building a game that teaches beginners to invest, the pivot from an AI trader and the brokerage partnerships ahead. The post Behind the Idea: Redvest appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Most people who start investing do it with real money and very little preparation. Redvest, a US gamified financial education platform, wants beginners to learn first: its app and website teach investing through games, quizzes, courses and competitions, then let users practise in a real-time stock market simulator using virtual money. The company says it has more than one million users across more than 40 countries.

Anya Ozmen, founder of Redvest

Its founder, Anya Ozmen, is a self-taught programmer who moved to the US from Turkey at 18 and built most of the product herself. In this Behind the Idea, she explains how an AI trading app turned down by the App Store became a learning platform, what growing it as a solo founder was like, and where Redvest goes next. The profit figures she gives for Redvest users are simulator results, made with virtual money rather than real trades.

Tell us more about your company and its offering

Redvest is a gamified financial education platform. Over 1 million Redvest users learn investing and finance with AI-powered games, competitions, courses and quizzes. Redvesters from 40+ countries have completed over 38,000 quizzes and generated over $500 million in order volume in the real-time stock market game. Our mission is to democratise access to financial education and empower Gen Zers to learn effectively by playing games, just like they did when they were kids!

What problem was your company set up to solve?

Around 80 per cent of retail investors lose money in the stock market, but 69 per cent to 83 per cent of Redvest users are profitable on our platform at any given time. Investing is easy, but making money is hard. Anyone can download Robinhood or Fidelity, but the majority lose money investing in the market, leaving them demotivated and one step behind on their financial journey. Redvest sets out to solve this problem by offering a risk-free, hands-on experience with AI-powered and data-driven gamified learning.

Since launch, how has your company evolved?

I built Redvest as an AI robo-adviser at first, as a fun side project when I was 23. It would automatically trade for you once you connected your brokerage account, using methods like value investing, technical trading and sentiment analysis according to your preferences and goals. When I submitted the app to the App Store, Apple actually didn’t accept it, so I ended up adding a stock market simulator to the platform to get it live on the App Store. However, when I put the app out there, I saw that people had a huge need for the learning piece. Users were completely lost about where to begin. They wanted to be able to control their trades, and no one was using the AI trader. All the attention was on the stock market simulator instead.

We pivoted to focusing on what our users needed and wanted the most. A couple of years later, we expanded to the web in addition to mobile and became the Duolingo of investing.

What has been the biggest challenge or most ‘tricky moment’ to overcome?

As a solo founder and self-taught developer, handling the initial growth was genuinely hard. In 2020, I started an AI software and mobile app development company, and through my work there, I taught myself how to program in a bunch of programming languages to help my team deliver client projects faster. I built and designed most of Redvest myself. It wasn’t as easy to build apps back then, and it took a lot longer to iterate. You needed to hand code all lines. There would be a bug, and I would stay up all night trying to fix it by myself without anyone to ask for advice. This taught me how to find and create resources for other people who might not have access to tools, information and large networks.

What are your biggest achievements or ‘proudest moment’ so far?

I’m proudest when we get an email from a customer about their positive experience, especially if it’s coupled with a new feature request! One specific moment of joy carved in my memory is when Redvest made the Top 30 for iOS in the Finance category. I saw Redvest’s logo next to big fintech companies’ logos, and I teared up. Having built most of the app and the website myself, it felt like seeing my kid graduate. I grew up in Turkey until I was 18, and my world was very small. I had never dreamt of anything big like this.

How would you describe the culture of your company?

Redvest’s company culture is focused on positivity and problem-solving. Our mission is to create tools that help and teach people while entertaining them, so the same applies to our team. Our team mostly consists of recent college graduates. My personal mission is to teach them as much as I can, setting them up for success in their career journeys. Most Fridays, we have a game hour as a team, playing games like Codenames, Pictionary and more!

What’s in store for the future?

Currently, we are working on some new and exciting partnerships with brokerages to bring educational tools to their platforms so that consumers coming to invest on those platforms can set themselves up for success.

title: Aldar and ADIB Launch Co-Branded Darna Covered Cards in Abu Dhabi
snippet: Aldar and ADIB have launched two Visa co-branded cards tied to the Darna loyalty programme, offering up to 10% back on retail and hospitality The post Aldar and ADIB Launch Co-Branded Darna Covered Cards in Abu Dhabi appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Aldar Properties and Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank (ADIB) have jointly launched a pair of co-branded covered cards linked to Aldar’s Darna digital loyalty programme, deepening the intersection of property, retail and Islamic banking in Abu Dhabi’s consumer market.

The two products, the ADIB Aldar Visa Infinite and the ADIB Aldar Visa Platinum Covered Cards, were issued on 21 October 2026. Both sit inside the Live Aldar app ecosystem, allowing cardholders to earn, track and redeem Darna Points across Aldar’s retail, hospitality, education and residential portfolio.

The product structure

The reward tiers are graduated. Cardholders earn up to 10% value back in Darna Points on eligible spending at participating Aldar malls, hotels, golf courses, restaurants and entertainment venues. Spending on Aldar property purchases and Aldar Education attracts up to 1.5%, while eligible international transactions earn up to 2%. Welcome bonuses of up to 20,000 Darna Points, equivalent to AED 1,000, are offered on sign-up, subject to card tier and qualifying conditions.

Additional benefits include complimentary Darna Gold or Platinum status depending on tier, access to more than 1,000 airport lounges worldwide, complimentary valet parking up to four times per month at selected UAE locations, and an annual fee waiver from the second year onwards for cardholders who meet defined spend thresholds: AED 30,000 in foreign currency or AED 75,000 in total transactions.

Faisal Falaknaz, group chief financial and sustainability officer at Aldar, said the partnership extends rewards to eligible property spend, “creating meaningful value around one of our customers’ most significant purchases.” Amit Malhotra, global head of retail banking at ADIB, framed the proposition as embedding banking more deeply into customers’ daily lives beyond traditional service relationships.

The cards are Sharia-compliant covered structures rather than conventional credit products, consistent with ADIB’s Islamic banking model. ADIB reported total assets of AED 304 billion as of June 2026, giving the partnership institutional weight within the UAE’s Islamic finance sector.

Market context and regulatory landscape

The co-branded card space in the Gulf has grown steadily as banks seek to deepen primary-account relationships and retailers look to translate loyalty programmes into payment data. The Aldar-ADIB structure is notable for spanning property purchasing alongside everyday retail, a combination that is less common than pure lifestyle or travel reward cards. Rewarding property transactions at the card level blurs the boundary between mortgage product and payment card, a wrinkle that sits within the DFSA and CBUAE regulatory perimeter for consumer credit and Islamic finance structures.

Visa’s involvement as the network rail gives the product global acceptance infrastructure, but the commercial logic is primarily domestic. Abu Dhabi’s real estate market has remained buoyant through 2025 and into 2026, driven by continued government investment and population growth, which provides a large addressable base for property-linked financial products.

Several UAE banks and property groups have experimented with similar closed-loop loyalty integrations, but the scale of Aldar’s landbank, which spans 76 million square metres, and the breadth of the Live Aldar app ecosystem give this proposition a wider earn-and-redeem surface than most comparable products in the region.

title: TransUnion: 81% of Digital Fraud Now Targets Existing Accounts
snippet: TransUnion's H1 2026 fraud report finds fraudsters shifting from identity creation to exploiting trusted customer relationships at scale. The post TransUnion: 81% of Digital Fraud Now Targets Existing Accounts appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
TransUnion has published its latest global Top Fraud Trends Report, covering the first half of 2026, and the headline finding reshapes how financial institutions and retailers should think about fraud exposure. Rather than fabricating new identities at the point of onboarding, fraudsters are now predominantly operating within established customer relationships: 81% of suspected digital fraud globally in H1 2026 occurred during interactions with existing customers.

The report, titled “Fraud in the Age of Continuous Trust”, is based on TransUnion’s proprietary transaction data and a June 2026 survey of business leaders across the US and international markets. Business leaders across sectors estimated fraud losses equivalent to nearly 7% of annual revenue over the past year, a figure that reflects both direct financial losses and the operational cost of remediation.

Phone spoofing and authorised fraud drive losses

Brian Killeen, VP of global identity solutions at TransUnion

Two communication-channel vulnerabilities stand out in the data. Nearly one in five outbound business-to-consumer calls made via US mobile carriers was spoofed in H1 2026, providing fraudsters with a mechanism to impersonate trusted brands and prompt account takeovers or payments. Separately, six in ten business leaders reported their customers were victimised by text spoofing in the past year.

These channels feed directly into authorised fraud, where a victim is manipulated into initiating a transaction or granting account access voluntarily. Scam and authorised fraud was cited as the leading source of losses by 35% of US business leaders and 29% globally, ahead of synthetic identity fraud (18% in both geographies), account takeover (16–17%) and first-party fraud (15–18%).

Brian Killeen, vice president of global identity solutions at TransUnion, said: “Harnessing intelligence across the customer lifecycle and applying context to each interaction is critical to identifying emerging threats and enabling trusted interactions.”

US lenders face an estimated $2.4 billion in exposure tied to synthetic identities as of 30 June 2026, and 67% of business leaders expect synthetic identity fraud to increase over the next two years. Fifty-three per cent described it as the threat they are least prepared to address.

AI lowers the cost of attack

The report identifies AI as the structural accelerant. Automation has reduced the unit economics of fraud by handling identity generation, content creation and victim targeting at a scale that previously required significant human effort. Forty-three per cent of US business leaders said the growing scale and sophistication of fraud is placing significant or severe pressure on their organisations.

The industry-level breakdown offers useful precision for risk teams. In financial services, transaction-related activity carries greater fraud risk than account creation, which underscores the need to connect identity, behavioural and transactional signals throughout the customer relationship. In retail, account creation is the primary risk vector given promotion abuse. In online gaming and betting, fraud risk is elevated across the full lifecycle, from bonus abuse at sign-up through account logins and withdrawals.

Regulatory and market read-across

The findings land against a backdrop of intensifying regulatory pressure on authorised push payment fraud. In the UK, the Payment Systems Regulator’s mandatory reimbursement framework, which came into force in October 2024, has put direct financial liability on payment service providers for qualifying APP fraud losses. That shifts the compliance calculus: fraud that exploits trusted channels is no longer simply a customer service problem but a balance-sheet risk for firms caught on the paying side of a spoofed instruction.

Across Europe, DORA’s operational resilience requirements and PSD3’s proposed enhancements to transaction monitoring will further raise the bar for how firms detect anomalies within established customer interactions, not just at onboarding. For financial institutions still calibrating their fraud tooling around front-door identity checks, the TransUnion data is a prompt to re-examine where in the customer lifecycle their defences are thinnest.

title: Arf and Ripple Bring RLUSD Settlement Liquidity to XRPL
snippet: Swiss-regulated Arf will supply short-duration working capital in RLUSD to licensed cross-border payment firms settling on the XRP Ledger. The post Arf and Ripple Bring RLUSD Settlement Liquidity to XRPL appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Arf, a Swiss-regulated financial institution headquartered in Zug, has partnered with Ripple to deliver stablecoin-denominated settlement liquidity to licensed cross-border payment companies operating on the XRP Ledger (XRPL). The arrangement uses Ripple’s RLUSD stablecoin as the working capital instrument and targets a structural problem that has dogged the cross-border payments industry for years: the timing mismatch between when a payment company must fund a transaction and when the underlying settlement actually arrives.

Arf reported that it has scaled to roughly $10 billion in annual global settlement volume since launching in November 2022, with capital turning over approximately four times a month. That velocity matters commercially: short-duration, high-turnover liquidity looks very different on a balance sheet and in a regulatory capital calculation than a traditional revolving credit line, which can take months to establish and typically demands collateral pledged in a single jurisdiction. For payment companies whose working capital needs to move across markets in step with payment flows, that mismatch is the core operational constraint the partnership is designed to address.

How the facility works

Ali Erhat Nalbant, co-founder and CEO at Arf

In the first phase, Arf will provide RLUSD liquidity directly on XRPL. Drawdowns are expected to be repaid within one to five business days as cross-border payments settle, allowing the same pool of capital to be recycled repeatedly against live payment flows. Arf retains underwriting and working capital decisions offchain, while XRPL provides the settlement rail.

A second phase is contingent on XRPL’s native lending infrastructure becoming operational. Once available, Arf says it intends to migrate more of its liquidity activity onto the protocol itself, enabling onchain capital management alongside its existing regulated treasury functions. No timeline for that infrastructure milestone was disclosed in the announcement.

Ali Erhat Nalbant, co-founder and chief executive of Arf, said the company is “meeting that need at scale, with $10 billion in annual settlement volume and capital turning over four times a month,” adding that the Ripple partnership is designed to help payment companies “bridge that gap and support more payment volume.”

Market and regulatory context

The announcement sits within the broader PayFi category, a term used to describe financial products structured around real-time payment flows and the time value of money, spanning settlement liquidity, receivables financing and fiat-to-stablecoin treasury management. Arf and Huma Finance are credited with coining the category; the partnership with Ripple extends Arf’s regulated infrastructure into a public blockchain environment.

RLUSD, Ripple’s dollar stablecoin, launched in late 2024 and is positioned as a regulated instrument for institutional settlement use cases rather than retail trading. Stablecoins used in payment settlement are increasingly subject to regulatory attention on both sides of the Atlantic. In the EU, the Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation covers asset-referenced and e-money tokens with specific capital and reserve requirements; in the UK, the Payment and Electronic Money Institution Regulations and the FCA‘s evolving stablecoin framework will shape how arrangements of this kind are treated domestically. Arf’s Swiss regulatory status under VQF membership provides a foundation for cross-border operation, though each market in which its liquidity is deployed will carry its own licensing considerations.

For payment operators evaluating the proposition, the key variables are the cost of RLUSD-denominated liquidity relative to existing bank credit, the jurisdictional reach of the facility, and the operational risk profile of a settlement rail that is partly onchain. The transition to native XRPL lending infrastructure, when it arrives, will shift some of that risk profile further onto the protocol layer and will be the more consequential development to watch.

title: Velera Says Credit Unions Can Learn Digital Money Together
snippet: Credit unions and industry partners can work together to understand where digital assets could be useful, Velera SVP, Emerging Services Scott P. Young writes in a new PYMNTS eBook, “Payments Leaders Rethink What Works in 2026.” At the start of 2026, the digital asset conversation was dominated by stablecoins. Market hype and fear of missing […] The post Velera Says Credit Unions Can Learn Digital Money Together appeared first on PYMNTS.com.
fullText:
At the start of 2026, the digital asset conversation was dominated by stablecoins. Market hype and fear of missing out (FOMO) were growing, while the GENIUS Act brought greater clarity to the regulatory path for payment stablecoins. Across the industry, financial institutions, FinTechs and payments companies were asking the same questions. Should we issue, integrate or partner?

I heard a similar urgency in my own conversations with credit union executives and boards. Could stablecoins become the next ChatGPT, with adoption accelerating before institutions were prepared? Could they drive member deposit outflows or cannibalize card interchange? Credit union leaders were looking to us for answers, but also for help identifying the questions they hadn’t thought to ask yet. Over the past nine months, I’ve heard many put it this way: “Tell me what I don’t know.”

That request gets to the heart of how I, and my department as a whole, approach emerging technologies at Velera: with curiosity and a willingness to challenge what we think we know, while learning and growing alongside our credit union partners. With stablecoins evolving so quickly, we wanted to get beyond the hype and understand what was actually taking shape across the digital asset space. To that end, my team and I brought together an inaugural cohort of credit unions, technology providers and other industry stakeholders to assess emerging technologies and use cases, evaluate potential partners, and explore the infrastructure and integrations needed to make digital assets viable for credit unions.

So far, the research and rapid shifts within the industry haven’t supported some of the more immediate concerns about stablecoins. We aren’t seeing strong peer-to-peer or point-of-sale applications, and concerns about material deposit outflows and card-interchange cannibalization have not been borne out so far. Instead, I’ve seen attention turning toward commercial applications, including B2B and cross-border payments, where digital assets may address clearer sources of friction.

The discussion is also expanding beyond just stablecoins to digital money more broadly. Stablecoins may offer advantages for certain use cases, while tokenized deposits present another approach, offering many blockchain-enabled capabilities while remaining connected to deposits held at regulated financial institutions and the existing banking framework.

That evolution raises another question. How can the industry avoid creating new silos?

If each institution develops a proprietary tokenized-deposit ecosystem, we could reproduce the fragmentation already present in traditional payments. Increasingly, I’m hearing conversations about shared infrastructure, interoperability, consortiums and networks that can connect institutions and move tokenized money at scale, something to which we at Velera are paying close attention.

As we move into Q4, my team and I will continue working with credit unions and industry partners to understand where digital assets could be useful and how different approaches might work together. There’s still a lot to learn, especially as new technologies and offerings are rapidly impacting the financial services industry. Our goal is not to chase every headline or claim certainty in an ever-evolving payments landscape. It is to listen, investigate and help credit unions prepare to act when the value becomes clear. Curiosity and collaboration are at the center of all we do and all we will continue to do.

title: Western Union, Intermex clash
snippet: The money transfer services company dropped its acquisition of the smaller rival after California regulators weighed in, but now a fight over the deal has ensued.
fullText:
Remittance services provider Western Union planned to buy International Money Express, but opted out Tuesday. Now, the two companies have begun a battle over whether the $500 million deal should be consummated.

Western Union had been waiting more than a year for regulators to approve a purchase of the younger rival also known as Intermex, but when the California Department of Financial Protection and Innovation issued approval conditions Tuesday, the acquirer backed out. Western Union decided against the deal and notified Intermex it was terminating the acquisition agreement on Tuesday, the day that was the deadline for either side to exit the pact.

The California regulator “delivered unacceptable final Conditions of Approval that would have required material changes to Western Union’s business model, its agent relationships and execution of its long-term business strategy,” Western Union said in a press release late Tuesday. 

Western Union’s move isn’t passing muster with Intermex, which notified Western Union on Wednesday that it expects the transaction to be completed. Now, a legal fight is brewing.

“Through its counsel, Intermex has responded to Western Union rejecting Western Union's purported termination of the merger agreement and demanding that Western Union take all actions necessary to consummate the merger,” Intermex said in its statement.

Denver-based Western Union, which provides cross-border payments services and has roots reaching back more than 100 years, announced in August 2025 that it would purchase Intermex, but since then the companies have been trying to gather needed regulatory approvals. Miami-based Intermex was founded in 1994.

“Western Union stands by its decision to terminate the merger agreement and disagrees with Intermex’s characterization of the termination,” a spokesperson for Western Union said by email. “Western Union believes it acted in accordance with the terms of the agreement and will respond as appropriate.”

While New York regulators reached an agreement with the companies for approval of the deal earlier this year, the companies still needed California’s input, given the states’ purview over money transfer businesses.

The California agency approved the deal Tuesday, but imposed conditions that it said were aimed at safeguarding consumers, preventing fraud, deterring money laundering and ensuring “ fair and competitive access to financial services.”

California called Western Union a major money transfer company used by Californians to send money to Mexico and Central America, but it also noted that Intermex is a significant player in the market, saying the merger would have “significant implications for California consumers.” 

To consummate the merger, the state regulator said in a Tuesday statement that the companies must “take certain steps,” that it didn’t specify in its public statement, “to detect and deter fraud.” 

The regulator also prohibited the companies from reducing the number of agent locations that provide services in California.Citing an existing court order requiring Western Union to thwart criminal use of its network, the regulator also called on the company to “adopt robust risk-based anti-fraud and anti-money laundering measures.”

The state department also underscored its conditions with a threat. “If Western Union consummates its transaction with Intermex and fails to comply with these conditions, DFPI can take enforcement actions that may lead to limitations on its business practices or suspension of its license,” California’s statement said. 

The state noted federal immigration policies under the Trump administration have affected the market. That negative impact from reduced immigration movement that leads migrant workers to send money to friends and family was clear last week during Western Union’s third-quarter earnings report. 

“The last 18 months have been a difficult period for the remittance industry, particularly for those of us with relatively large retail franchises in the Americas,” Western Union CEO Devin McGranahan said during a webcast with analysts. “We have seen both an overall decline in the retail market and an acceleration of the shift towards digital.”

As part of its cost-cutting and shift to more digital operations, McGranahan said that Western Union had eliminated 500 full-time employees and has started a voluntary retirement program that it expects to lead to 150 more employee departures. 

At the end of last year, the company had about 9,600 workers worldwide, according to its annual filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

fullText:
Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

G7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sector 

CMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

fullText:
Patients call a hospital to move an appointment, refill a prescription or ask about a bill. At MUSC Health, those calls frustrated patients and strained staff.

The Medical University of South Carolina’s health system now sends them first to Emily, an artificial intelligence (AI) agent built on SoundHound AI’s platform. Emily has supported more than 2.2 million patient calls since MUSC Health deployed it in 2024, SoundHound said in a July announcement. That month, MUSC Health added its retail and specialty pharmacy phone lines. Patients can ask Emily to request a prescription refill, check a refill’s status or find pharmacy hours and locations.

Before Emily, the call center was open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and the system wanted 24-hour support, Crystal Broj, chief digital transformation officer at MUSC Health, told HealthTech magazine in August. She cited “patient frustration, workforce pressure” and a need to modernize. Emily is integrated with MUSC Health’s Epic electronic health record, so a changed appointment updates the patient’s record automatically, the magazine reported.

Emily Answers All 92 Patient Access Phone Lines

Emily started with two tasks and now answers all 92 of MUSC Health’s patient access phone lines, according to HealthTech Hot Spot. The first tasks were confirming and canceling appointments, Broj said in a March interview with HealthTech HotSpot at the HIMSS conference. Rescheduling came next, then Spanish-language calls.

Emily now handles 25% of MUSC Health’s patient calls, Broj told Chief Healthcare Executive in June. Staff answer the rest faster and fewer callers hang up, she said. Patients who want a live person can still reach one.

Bill Payments and Refill Requests Move to Emily

Emily also answers billing questions and helps patients pay a bill. A caller can ask to schedule an appointment and pay a bill in one call, and Emily completes the first before raising the second. “She can switch that mode and remember what you wanted to talk about,” Broj told HealthTech HotSpot.

Additionally, Emily can handle pharmaceutical refill requests, give a real-time status update and route the caller to a pharmacy team when needed. The technology has to be “secure, reliable and capable of responsibly managing sensitive patient interactions,” Broj said in the July announcement.

In Utah, AI is going a step further and signing off on some refills itself. Regulators there cleared Legion Health to let its AI renew some psychiatric medications without a physician approving each one, PYMNTS reported in April.

60% of Healthcare Firms Use AI Customer Service Chatbots

Customer service is the most commonplace healthcare firms use AI. Sixty percent use it for customer service chatbots, the PYMNTS Intelligence report “Financial Services Pulls Ahead in the Enterprise AI Race” found. The May report is based on a March survey of 60 senior technology executives at U.S. enterprises with at least $1 billion in annual revenue, 20 of them in healthcare.

Spending is following. Twenty-seven percent of health systems pay for commercial AI licenses, triple the rate across the U.S. economy, PYMNTS reported in January, citing a Menlo Ventures and Morning Consult survey.

Sixty percent of healthcare firms plan to raise AI budgets over the next 12 months, the PYMNTS Intelligence report found. However, obstacles remain. Thirty percent named system integration challenges as a top AI barrier, and the same share named data quality issues. Customer journey orchestration, the coordination of every patient interaction from first contact to ongoing care, is at 5% adoption in healthcare, the lowest figure in the survey.

title: Finom adds MCP Connection for Claude and ChatGPT Account Queries
snippet: The European SME finance platform has launched a read-only Model Context Protocol link letting businesses query accounts from inside AI assistants. The post Finom adds MCP Connection for Claude and ChatGPT Account Queries appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Finom, the Amsterdam-headquartered financial platform for European SMEs, has launched Finom MCP, a read-only connection built on the open Model Context Protocol (MCP) standard that allows customers to query their Finom business accounts from inside Claude or ChatGPT using plain-language prompts.

The feature is included across all Finom plans and is rolling out pan-EU from today, 22 October 2026. At launch, customers can interrogate transactions, wallets, invoices, cards and accounting data, and request a morning briefing of recent business activity, without leaving their AI assistant.

What it does and what it deliberately does not

Kristjan Kaar, CPO at Finom

The read-only scope is a considered design choice rather than a capability gap. Both Claude and ChatGPT explicitly prohibit write actions that would result in money movement, and Finom’s own position is that trust in an AI-connected financial product must be established through progressive disclosure. The connection will not move funds, issue cards or alter account settings at launch.

Kristjan Kaar, Finom’s chief product officer, acknowledged that the company is not the first mover in this space. “We are not the first to public MCP and we will not pretend to be,” he said. “We’re starting with a first set of read-only access, with write capabilities to follow, all built on an open standard rather than a walled garden.”

Access is controlled entirely by the customer. The connection is initiated from within the assistant itself, redirecting users to a Finom-hosted consent screen where they authenticate with their existing Finom credentials. Role-scoped access means a user can only surface data their Finom account already permits them to see, and the connection can be revoked at any time. No credentials are passed to the AI provider.

Finom’s CAIO and co-founder Ivo Dimitrov framed the engineering priority as boundary design rather than model sophistication. “The engineering that matters here is not the model, it is the boundaries around it: your own login, access scoped to the role you already have, nothing shared beyond what you ask, and the ability to switch it off.”

The company is transparent that AI-generated answers may contain errors; the Finom app remains the authoritative record for official statements and reporting. Data retrieved through MCP is processed under the customer’s own agreement with their AI provider.

Market context and regulatory read-across

Finom’s own media FAQ names Qonto and Pennylane as firms that reached public MCP integrations first, which is an unusual degree of candour for a product launch announcement. The MCP standard, backed by Anthropic and gaining traction across enterprise tooling, is emerging as the practical mechanism by which AI assistants will connect to the business-software stack, much as OAuth became the standard handshake for web services. Early adoption of the open protocol, rather than building a proprietary integration, positions Finom to extend the connection to additional product areas without renegotiating closed partnerships.

For regulators, the architecture matters. Finom holds an Electronic Money Institution licence issued by De Nederlandsche Bank and operates within the EU’s PSD2 framework, which already mandates open APIs for account data access. An MCP layer built on top of regulated API access sits closer to the spirit of open finance than a screen-scraping or credential-sharing model. The phased approach, read access first, then user-confirmed write actions with secure authentication, mirrors the strong customer authentication logic that PSD2 and the incoming PSD3 regime apply to payment initiation.

Finom raised a 115 million euro Series C in June 2025, bringing total funding to more than 300 million euros. The company serves more than 300,000 businesses across Europe. The next phase of Finom MCP, in which the assistant prepares actions for the customer to confirm rather than simply answering questions, has no published timeline.

title: Rechitta V2 Adds Chat Mode after 100,000 Minutes of Broker Use

fullText:
Rechitta, a Dubai-based AI platform serving real estate brokers, has launched its V2 product update after recording 100,000 minutes of usage across its existing broker base. The milestone is being used by the company to validate the platform’s core proposition: replacing brochures, callback queues and scattered project documentation with a single AI-driven interface fed by verified developer data.

The V2 release centres on two interaction modes. Presentation Mode guides brokers through a project at their own pace, allowing them to scroll through visual assets and live project details while posing questions. The newly added Chat Mode is designed for situations where a spoken or guided session is impractical, such as when a broker is already on a call with a client or attending a busy sales event. Typed queries return instant answers on unit pricing, payment plans and handover dates, drawn from the same verified developer data that underpins the presentation layer.

Co-founder Aryaman Maheshwari said the 100,000-minute figure was significant because it reflected genuine engagement rather than passive sign-ups. “Those interactions have taught us how people actually want to explore, understand and question real estate projects,” he said. “V2 is a direct evolution of the product based on that behaviour.”

Co-founder Atiksh Mittal added that the update was intended to make the platform more conversational without removing the broker from the centre of the sales process.

The release also introduces the Rechitta Orb, a visual identity element the company says will serve as the recognisable interface for the AI assistant across both modes.

Market context

Rechitta sits within a broader category of AI-assisted sales enablement tools that have expanded quickly across Gulf real estate over the past two years. Dubai’s off-plan property market, which accounts for a substantial share of residential transaction volumes, creates particular information-management pressure: brokers routinely handle multiple concurrent project portfolios, each with distinct payment plan structures, handover schedules and unit availability that changes in near real time.

Several regional proptech firms and global CRM providers have moved to embed AI-powered Q&A and document-retrieval functions into broker workflows, though the verified-data angle Rechitta emphasises, where content originates directly from the developer rather than from scraped listings, represents a defensible point of differentiation if the developer onboarding pipeline can scale.

The broader regulatory environment for AI-powered sales tools in the UAE remains relatively permissive, with the Dubai Land Department actively encouraging digital transformation across the real estate transaction chain. However, the use of AI to communicate pricing and availability to brokers who then pass that information to buyers carries an implicit accuracy obligation, particularly as off-plan disputes in the emirate have drawn periodic regulatory attention.

Regulatory and commercial path

Rechitta has not disclosed the number of developers currently integrated onto the platform, the size of its broker user base, or whether it operates on a subscription, per-project or revenue-share commercial model. Those details matter for assessing whether 100,000 usage minutes represents a concentrated proof-of-concept with a small number of power users or a more distributed adoption curve across the market.

The next meaningful milestones to watch are developer count, geographic expansion beyond Dubai, and whether the company pursues external funding to accelerate integrations. Rechitta V2 is live now; a product walkthrough is available on the company’s website.

A multistate settlement that 43 states reached with rent-to-own company Acima Digital requires the firm to address practices that the states alleged included misleading consumers about its agreements and deceptively marking up prices, the Office of the Attorney General of Connecticut said in a Thursday (Nov. 12) press release.

Acima and several state attorneys general announced the $183.5 million settlement Thursday, saying it resolved a five-year investigation into the company’s rent-to-own financing practices.

The 43 states involved in the settlement alleged that Acima marketed its rental-purchase agreements as 90-day pay off programs without disclosing that consumers were automatically defaulted into a maximum 12-month term in which they could pay about twice the cash price advertised by Acima’s retail partner; misled consumers into believing that they were obtaining traditional financing by using terms like “credit” when advertising its rental-purchase product; further obscured the terms of the transaction during its process for electronically executing rental-purchase agreements; and obstructed consumers’ ability to terminate their rental-purchase agreements without penalty by returning their merchandise to Acima, according to the press release.

The settlement requires Acima to address these practices by, among other things, refraining from making certain representations in its advertising unless other material information is clearly and conspicuously disclosed; refraining from obscuring the material terms and conditions of its rental-purchase agreements during its electronic signature process; and refraining from obstructing consumers’ ability to terminate their rental-purchase agreements by returning the merchandise to Acima, per the release.

Acima Digital and Acima Holdings, which are wholly owned subsidiaries of Upbound Group, said in a Thursday press release that the settlement resolves a multistate investigation that began in 2021 and that the company is dedicated to transparency, fairness and compliance with applicable laws.

“By agreeing to the settlement, which does not include findings or admissions of wrongdoing, Acima resolves a longstanding matter, allowing the company to focus on serving its customers and retailers and continue growing its business,” the company said in the release.

Connecticut Attorney General William Tong said in his office’s Thursday press release: “Our settlement sends millions of dollars back to consumers and forces strict reforms to ensure fair and honest practices going forward.”

Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson said in a Thursday press release: “Companies cannot use misleading advertising or hidden costs to take advantage of consumers.”

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in a Thursday press release: “Acima exploited Virginians through predatory leasing practices dressed up as flexible payment options. title: Maersk’s Legacy-System Incident Shows M&A’s New Cyber Requirement

fullText:
Shipping giant A.P. Moller-Maersk disclosed Wednesday (Nov. 11) that an unauthorized party accessed and extracted data from a legacy IT system inherited through a previous acquisition.

Maersk has not reported a companywide compromise, but the incident illustrates a persistent problem for acquisitive businesses. Technology inherited through M&A can remain an operational and security obligation long after the transaction’s financial benefits have been incorporated into performance expectations.

The company said its investigation remains ongoing, with preliminary findings suggesting no sensitive data was disclosed and no indication of disruption to its broader operations or connected customer systems.

Read more: After 20 Years of ERP Consolidation, M&A Still Moves Faster Than Integration 

Integration Savings Can Become Deferred Costs

M&A integration is typically evaluated through cost savings, efficiencies and the consolidating overlapping functions. Technology rationalization is often central to those targets. But acquired systems can remain in service because they support specialized workflows, contain difficult-to-migrate data or connect to customers and suppliers who depend on established processes.

For dealmakers, leaving inherited systems untouched can also be economically rational. Migrating data, replacing specialized applications and disrupting established workflows all carry costs. But the decision to defer modernization can create obligations that outlast the integration program, turning what initially looks like a cost saving into a recurring expense.

The PYMNTS Intelligence report “Scale Amplification: How Revenue Amplifies Agent-Driven Identity,” showed that large enterprises, with their larger digital footprints, can be more susceptible to today’s new artificial intelligence-powered attacks favored by adversarial fraudsters.

Maersk did not immediately reply to PYMNTS’ request for comment, but the company reported in its statement that there was no indication the intrusion spread into other systems or affected customers and partners connected through APIs and electronic data interchange. Assuming those findings hold, the incident would also demonstrate the value of containing risk within a discrete environment.

See also: The M&A Files: You Just Had an Acquisition — Now What?

Cross-Jurisdiction Supply Chain Can Make the Stakes Larger

For logistics companies, the consequences of inherited technology extend beyond the acquiring organization. Shipping and fulfillment platforms connect carriers, warehouses, customs intermediaries, suppliers and customers through overlapping systems and data exchanges.

Even when an incident does not disrupt physical operations, information held in those environments can create risks involving commercial confidentiality, customer relationships and fraudulent communications.

That makes the distinction between operational resilience and data protection particularly important.

“It’s not about abandoning legacy systems, but modernizing around them intelligently,” Garrett Baird, vice president of product, banking and FinTech at Paymentus, told PYMNTS in an interview published in May.

And the PYMNTS Intelligence tracker “Who Decides Now: How Developers and Tech Teams Are Reshaping the Future of AP Payments” found in July that 58% of small to medium-sized businesses rank integration as very or extremely important when evaluating technology solutions.

title: Why PayPal wants to have a bank
snippet: The digital payments company would tap a bank subsidiary for lending to its merchants, but also to diversify its sources of capital.
fullText:
PayPal Holdings still sees advantages from winning a bank charter as the digital payments giant’s new CEO pursues a transformation of the company.

That’s according to the company’s chief financial and operating officer, Jamie Miller, who talked about PayPal’s bank charter application at the KBW Fintech Ecosystem Conference this week.

When Miller was asked by the analyst hosting the event to comment on PayPal’s effort to form an industrial bank, she explained how it would play into PayPal’s plan to provide more financial services, such as lending to its millions of merchant clients.

She pointed to the “merchant lending that underpins our work,” saying the company’s processing support for small businesses, sole proprietors and micro-sellers are all able to partake of its lending services.

San Jose, California-based PayPal filed applications with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. and the Utah Department of Financial Institutions last December to establish a Utah-chartered industrial loan company back when Alex Chriss was CEO. But Chriss has since exited, with Enrique Lores taking that top post this past March.

Lores has continued to pursue a strategy offering more financial services to PayPal’s 400 million consumer customers and its 20 million merchant clients. Financial services that the company is spooling up include increased buy now, pay later lending under the PayPal Pay Later brand as well new services via its peer-to-peer payments tool Venmo. 

As part of PayPal’s restructuring plan begun in April, Lores has cut some 2,000 employee jobs, shaved management layers and reorganized the business into three key divisions: checkout and PayPal; consumer financial services and Venmo; and processing, payment services and crypto. 

The company expects to take about $1.5 billion in costs out of the business in the next two to three years, Miller said.

Miller also suggested a bank operation would be advantageous as another route to capital. “The other side of it is to diversify our funding sources,” she said at the event. 

“We've been building out a variety of different funding sources,” Miller said. “We fund a lot through our own free cash flow and our cash on balance sheet, but we've also begun taking books off balance sheet in Europe and in the U.S. to really just diversify where the cash and funding sources come from.”

Last year, PayPal sold the investment firm KKR some of its buy now, pay later loan receivables originated in France, Germany, the United Kingdom and other European countries. 

To the extent that a PayPal bank could take in consumer or commercial deposits that could also be a new source of capital, the CFO said. “Certainly, deposits are another cost-efficient way” to diversify the company’s capital sources, she said.

PayPal’s application for a bank charter is part of a wave of payments companies seeking to form banks. Others include pay later provider Affirm Holdings, which sought FDIC and Nevada bank charters this year, as well as mega-processor Fiserv and digital juggernaut Stripe, which have won special Georgia bank charters.

Miller doesn’t anticipate the company’s balance sheet approach changing if it does win the option to establish the bank.

“We continue to expect to be generally balance sheet light,” she said. “We're going to make choices around what the right return profile will be around when we keep it on balance sheet versus when we take it off.”

She didn’t provide any update on regulators’ response to the company’s application.

Small businesses are finding room to take on more work without adding staff, and their artificial intelligence-related staffing decisions more often involve a hire they didn’t make than a worker they let go.

The PYMNTS Intelligence report “New Data Shows Small Businesses Use AI to Grow Without Hiring,” published in October, was based on a survey of 533 small- to medium-sized businesses (SMBs) in the United States. It examined how AI affected daily work, finances and staffing decisions.

The report found that 74% of SMBs use AI at least occasionally. Among businesses that have used it, 60% said they produce more work without adding staff, and 72% said they finish tasks faster. For an owner trying to serve more customers with the same team, AI can act like an extra pair of hands. The findings suggest businesses have opportunities to expand their capacity without immediately taking on the recurring expense of another employee.

Key findings from the report:

Skipped hires are more common than layoffs. Among AI users, 13% skipped a full-time hire they otherwise would have made, compared with 3.3% who laid off someone because of AI. That’s a 9.7-percentage-point difference. Overall, 26% took at least one of four staffing actions, including skipping a hire, cutting hours or a role, ending or not renewing an arrangement, or laying someone off. Roughly three-quarters reported none of those changes.

Growing businesses are also reconsidering their next hire. Among AI users whose revenue increased, 16% skipped a full-time hire, compared with 10% of those whose revenue stayed flat. Layoffs remained uncommon in both groups, at 4% and 2.2%, respectively. The pattern suggests AI-related staffing decisions extend beyond businesses facing weak sales. Owners with growing revenue are also finding ways to handle work without filling every position they previously expected to add.

The gains include work businesses couldn’t previously handle. Some 45% of AI users said the technology let them take on assignments beyond their previous capabilities. Customer service was the most common application, followed by marketing, bookkeeping and sales. These everyday uses help explain how AI can increase output across a small company. Using the technology for these functions, however, doesn’t necessarily mean a business replaced a paid worker.

The report also revealed opportunities for businesses selling human expertise. Some 23% gained customers who specifically wanted a person doing the work, while 14% picked up assignments fixing AI-generated output. These findings suggest owners can use AI to improve internal efficiency while continuing to sell services customers want people to deliver.

AI can create new work even as it changes how businesses decide who does it.
